summary: Chinese nouns have no grammatical gender, and nothing agrees with a noun: 这本书, 这张桌子, 这个女孩 — 这 never changes. The sex of people is said with different words (男人 / 女人, 男孩 / 女孩) or with 男 / 女 before a noun (男老师 ‘male teacher’, 女学生 ‘female student’); ‘he’ and ‘she’ differ only in writing (他 / 她, both tā). What every noun has instead is its measure word — learn 一本书, 一张桌子 the way you learn der Tisch, das Buch.

blocks.caption: Gender in the course languages

blocks.title: The measure word is the ‘gender’ of Chinese
blocks.text: Not grammatically, but in practice: it is the extra thing you must know about every noun, and it groups nouns by shape and kind (张: flat; 把: with a handle; 本: bound).

blocks.title: Male or female people
blocks.text: 男 / 女 before a noun: 男老师, 女老师, 男学生, 女学生; and pairs of words: 男人 / 女人, 男孩 / 女孩.

blocks.title: Don’t carry gender over
blocks.text: There is no ‘feminine’ form of 老师 or 学生 to look for: 她是老师 is complete.

askYourself: Do I need a gender or an agreeing ending? → never in Chinese.
Is it a person whose sex matters? → a separate word (男孩 / 女孩) or 男 / 女 before the noun.
Writing ‘he / she / it’? → 他 / 她 / 它 — all tā.
What does this noun need instead? → its measure word (一本书, 一张桌子).

traps: Looking for a feminine ending: there is none — a female teacher is 女老师.
Thinking 这 changes for gender or number: 这个男孩, 这个女孩 — the same 这个.

quiz.q: How many grammatical genders do Chinese nouns have?
quiz.why: Chinese has no gender; nothing agrees with the noun.

quiz.q: What do you learn with every Chinese noun instead of a gender?
quiz.why: 一本书, 一张桌子, 一把椅子.

quiz.q: 这个男孩 / 这个女孩 — does 这个 change?

notes.text: Greek nouns have three genders shown by the article (ο, η, το), and articles and adjectives agree. Chinese has none of this: no gender to learn, and a measure word per noun instead (ένα τραπέζι ~ 一张桌子).
Russian has three genders and agreement everywhere (новый стол, новая книга); Chinese 新 never changes. Feminine forms like учительница have no Chinese match: 老师, or 女老师 when it matters.
Spanish has two genders (el libro, la mesa) and many paired forms (profesor / profesora); Chinese has no gender and marks sex only when needed, with 男 / 女: 男老师, 女老师.

English nouns have no grammatical gender either; only he / she / it show sex — and in Chinese even these sound the same (tā). Pairs like waiter / waitress correspond to 男 / 女 + noun, used only when it matters.
French has two genders and agreement (un grand livre, une grande table); Chinese 大 never changes. Le professeur / la professeure: Chinese says 老师 for both.
German der / die / das is a gender to learn with every noun; Chinese has none, but its measure word (一本书, 一张桌子) is the one extra thing to learn per noun.
Hindi has two genders, and adjectives and verbs agree (अच्छा लड़का / अच्छी लड़की); Chinese 好 never changes: 好男孩, 好女孩.
Persian has no grammatical gender either, and u is ‘he’ and ‘she’ alike — Chinese spoken tā is the same idea.
Marathi has three genders (masculine, feminine, neuter) with agreement in adjectives and verbs; Chinese has none.
Arabic has two genders with agreement in verbs, adjectives, pronouns and numbers; Chinese marks none of it.
Hebrew has two genders with agreement in adjectives, verbs and even ‘you’; Chinese marks none of it — only the written 他 / 她.
Turkish has no grammatical gender, and o is he / she / it; Chinese works the same way in speech and adds the measure word as the new thing to learn.
Japanese has no grammatical gender either; and like Japanese counters, Chinese measure words sort nouns by shape and kind.
Korean has no grammatical gender; Chinese neither — only the written 他 / 她 differ.
Finnish has no grammatical gender (hän = he / she); Chinese neither, and its tā has gender only in writing.
Hungarian has no grammatical gender (ő = he / she); Chinese neither — spoken tā is the same idea.

Swahili has noun classes (m- / wa- for people, ki- / vi- for many things …) with agreement in every word; Chinese has no classes and no agreement, but its measure words also sort nouns by kind (个, 本, 张).
Luganda has about ten pairs of noun classes (omu- / aba-, eki- / ebi- …) with agreement through the sentence; Chinese has neither, but measure words do sort nouns by kind.
Vietnamese has no gender either, and its classifiers play the same role as Chinese measure words.
Inuktitut has no grammatical gender; neither has Chinese.

seeAlso.note: German has three genders shown by the article (der Tisch, die Tür, das Buch); Chinese has none — but a measure word per noun.
Arabic has two genders, mostly visible in the ending -a (ة); adjectives and verbs agree — nothing agrees in Chinese.
Hebrew has two genders (feminine often -a / -et); verbs and adjectives agree — Chinese marks no gender at all.
